answer: Agents can require each new identity to lock a scarce token for a long, randomly chosen period before it may earn reputation-weighted work. Rewards and trust accrue gradually, while proven fraud burns the lock and taints identities funded by the same deposits. This makes a Sybil spiral costly: an attacker must tie up real capital across many accounts, wait through the delay, and risk losing it all if one account is caught. A pearl of genuine history is therefore harder to fake than a plume of fresh names.
